title: Kotlin Programming with IntelliJ IDEA
subtitle: Write concise, null-safe Kotlin in IntelliJ IDEA: functions and lambdas, data and sealed classes, collections, coroutines, tests, and code that works hand in hand with Java.
outcomes: Set up Kotlin projects built with Gradle in IntelliJ IDEA, and run and test them from the IDE
Write idiomatic Kotlin with val and var, type inference, null safety and when expressions
Process data concisely with functions, extension functions, lambdas and collection operations
Model data with classes, data classes, sealed classes and objects
Run concurrent work with coroutines, test with kotlin.test, and mix Kotlin with Java, converting Java files in the IDE
prerequisites: Some programming experience in any language: variables, functions, loops and classes. Java experience helps in the last module but isn't required. IntelliJ IDEA (the free version is enough) on Windows, macOS or Linux; it supports Kotlin and Gradle out of the box and can download a JDK for you.
description: Kotlin is a modern, concise language for the JVM, used for Android apps, back-end services and tools, and it works hand in hand with Java. This course is for people who can already program and want to write Kotlin well, in IntelliJ IDEA, the IDE from the company that created the language. Each lesson teaches a Kotlin idea and then shows it in the IDE, step by step, with the keyboard shortcuts for macOS, Windows and Linux. You'll set up Gradle projects and see how Kotlin's type system keeps null under control, write functions, extension functions and lambdas, and process data with Kotlin's collection operations. You'll model data with data classes, sealed hierarchies and objects, run work concurrently with coroutines, and test it all with kotlin.test. Finally you'll mix Kotlin with Java, calling each from the other and converting Java files to Kotlin in the IDE. Every module ends with a hands-on lab, and the course ends with a payment-processing project that you build yourself.

modules.title: Kotlin, Gradle and null safety
modules.summary: Create a Kotlin project built with Gradle, meet Kotlin's types, val and var and its expressions, and see how the type system keeps null out of places where it doesn't belong.

lessons.title: A Kotlin project with Gradle
objectives: Create a Kotlin project with Gradle in IntelliJ IDEA
Explain what build.gradle.kts and the Gradle wrapper do
Run code and Gradle tasks from the IDE
key_points: Kotlin is a statically typed language created by JetBrains. On the JVM it compiles to the same kind of bytecode as Java, so Kotlin and Java code and libraries can be used together in one project.
Gradle is a build tool. A Kotlin project's build is described in build.gradle.kts, written in Gradle's Kotlin DSL, and settings.gradle.kts names the project.

The kotlin("jvm") plugin compiles Kotlin for the JVM. Dependencies are added with implementation(...) for the program and testImplementation(...) for tests, and mavenCentral() says where to download them from.
The Gradle wrapper (the gradlew scripts and the gradle/wrapper folder) downloads and runs the Gradle version the project expects, so nobody has to install Gradle themselves.
A Kotlin program starts in a top-level fun main(), with no class needed around it; code goes in src/main/kotlin and tests in src/test/kotlin.

lessons.title: val, var, types and expressions
objectives: Declare read-only and mutable variables and let Kotlin infer their types
Use if and when as expressions, string templates and ranges
key_points: val declares a read-only variable that can't be reassigned, and var a mutable one. Prefer val, and use var only when a value really has to change.
Kotlin infers types from values, as in val count = 3 (an Int), but you can write them out: val ratio: Double = 0.5. Numbers are never converted implicitly, so use toLong(), toDouble() and so on.
String templates put values into text, as in "$name has ${items.size} items", and a triple-quoted string can span several lines.
if and when are expressions that return a value: val size = when { n < 10 -> "small"; n < 100 -> "medium"; else -> "large" }.
Ranges describe sequences of numbers: 1..5 includes 5, 1..<5 (or 1 until 5) stops before it, and 10 downTo 0 step 2 counts down; x in 1..5 tests whether x is in the range.
== compares values by calling equals, while === checks whether two references point to the same object.

steps.do: In Main.kt, declare a few values without types. Put the caret on one and open its quick documentation to see the type Kotlin inferred.
steps.code:
val count = 3
val ratio = count / 2.0
val label = "Count: $count, ratio: $ratio"
steps.see: count is an Int, ratio a Double and label a String.

lessons.title: Null safety
objectives: Explain how Kotlin's nullable types prevent null pointer errors
Handle nullable values with safe calls, the Elvis operator, smart casts and let
key_points: Types don't allow null unless they say so: a String always holds a string, while a String? may be null, and the compiler won't let you call a method on a String? until null is handled.
The safe-call operator ?. gives null instead of failing, as in name?.length, and the Elvis operator ?: supplies a fallback: name?.length ?: 0.
After a check such as if (name != null), the compiler smart-casts name to String inside the block, so it can be used directly.
The not-null assertion !! turns a nullable value into a non-null one and throws a NullPointerException if it's null; use it rarely, only where null really is impossible.
Many standard functions return null instead of throwing, such as "42".toIntOrNull(), list.firstOrNull() and map[key], and they pair naturally with ?: and let.
value?.let { ... } runs a block only when value isn't null, with the value available inside the block as it.

steps.do: Write a function that takes a String? and calls a method on it.
steps.see: name.uppercase() is red: only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver.

steps.do: Put the caret on the error and open Show Context Actions. The fixes include a safe call, a non-null assertion and surrounding the code with a null check: choose the safe call.

modules.title: Functions, lambdas and collections
modules.summary: Write functions the Kotlin way, with default and named arguments, expression bodies and extension functions; pass behaviour around with lambdas; and process data with Kotlin's collection operations.

lessons.title: Functions and extension functions
objectives: Write functions with default and named arguments and expression bodies
Add behaviour to existing types with extension functions
key_points: Functions are declared with fun, each parameter as name: Type, and the return type after the brackets: fun area(w: Double, h: Double): Double = w * h is a function with an expression body.
Default arguments replace most overloads, as in fun greet(name: String, greeting: String = "Hello"), and callers can name arguments: greet("Ada", greeting = "Hi").
Functions can live at the top level of a file, outside any class. A function that returns nothing useful returns Unit, which you don't need to write.
An extension function adds a function to an existing type without changing it: fun String.initials() = split(" ").joinToString("") { it.take(1).uppercase() } is called as "ada lovelace".initials().
Extensions are chosen when compiling, from the declared type, and they can't reach the type's private members: they're a tidy way to add helpers, not a way to change a class.

Run it.

lessons.title: Lambdas and higher-order functions
objectives: Write lambdas and pass them to higher-order functions
Use function types, trailing lambdas and function references
Choose a scope function: let, apply, also or run
key_points: A lambda is a function written in braces: { a: Int, b: Int -> a + b }. When it has a single parameter you can leave the parameter out and refer to it as it, as in { it * 2 }.
A higher-order function takes or returns a function. A parameter of a function type, such as (Int) -> Boolean, is called like any other function.
When a lambda is the last argument it can go outside the brackets, as a trailing lambda: numbers.filter { it > 0 }. When it's the only argument, the brackets can go too.
A function reference passes an existing function as a value: ::isEven for a top-level function, String::length for a member, or a bound reference such as log::add.
Scope functions run a block on an object: let and run return the block's result, and apply and also return the object itself. apply suits configuring an object, and let suits nullable values.
Unlike Java's, Kotlin lambdas can change the local variables they capture, such as a counter declared outside them.

Run it.

lessons.title: Working with collections
objectives: Choose between read-only and mutable collections
Transform, filter, group and aggregate collections with their operations
Inspect collection chains in the debugger
key_points: listOf, setOf and mapOf create read-only collections, and mutableListOf, mutableSetOf and mutableMapOf create mutable ones; a read-only List can't be changed through that reference.
Operations such as filter, map, sortedBy, take and distinct return new collections, while sum, sumOf { it.amountCents }, count { ... }, maxByOrNull { ... } and fold return a single value.
groupBy { it.country } gives a Map<String, List<T>>, associateBy { it.id } a map from a key to each element, and partition a pair of lists: the elements that match and the rest.
map[key] returns null for a missing key, while getValue(key) throws; for ((key, value) in map) visits every entry.
A sequence, from asSequence(), works lazily, one element at a time, which avoids building an intermediate list at every step of a long chain over a lot of data.

Run it.

modules.title: Classes, data classes, sealed classes and objects
modules.summary: Model a domain the Kotlin way: classes with primary constructors and properties, data classes for values, sealed hierarchies that when can check completely, and objects for single instances.

lessons.title: Classes, properties and constructors
objectives: Write classes with primary constructors, properties and init blocks
Control inheritance and visibility
key_points: A primary constructor goes in the class header and can declare properties at once, as in class Account(val id: String, var owner: String); init blocks run when an object is created.

Properties replace fields with getters and setters: account.balanceCents reads one, a custom get() or set(value) can compute or check values, and private set makes a property read-only outside the class.
Classes and their members are final by default. Mark a class open to allow subclasses, and a member open to allow overriding, which subclasses do with override.

require(amount > 0) { "amount must be positive" } throws IllegalArgumentException with that message when the condition is false, which suits checking arguments; check(...) does the same for state, with IllegalStateException.
Visibility modifiers are public (the default), internal (visible within the same module), protected and private. Objects are created without new: val account = Account("A-1").

steps.do: Write a class with a primary constructor, a property with a private setter, and an init block.
Try to extend it: class SavingsAccount(id: String) : Account(id). Account is final, so the editor reports an error, and Show Context Actions offers to make Account open.
Inside a class, open Generate to add toString(), equals() and hashCode(), a secondary constructor or overrides.
See the class's members in the file structure popup.
See what Java sees: with the file open, choose Tools | Kotlin | Show Kotlin Bytecode, then click Decompile.

lessons.title: Data classes and enum classes
objectives: Model values with data classes, and copy and destructure them
Use enum classes with when expressions that cover every case
key_points: A data class holds data: data class Payment(val id: String, val amountCents: Long) gets equals, hashCode, toString, copy and componentN functions, generated from its primary constructor's properties.
Two data class instances with equal properties are equal: Payment("p1", 100) == Payment("p1", 100) is true, whereas ordinary classes compare identity unless they override equals.
copy makes a changed copy of an immutable object, as in payment.copy(amountCents = 500). With val properties, data classes are safe to share and to use as map keys or set elements.
Destructuring unpacks a data class into variables, in the order of its constructor's properties: val (id, amount) = payment.
An enum class defines a fixed set of constants, as in enum class Status { PENDING, APPROVED, DECLINED }. Status.entries lists them, and a when over an enum with no else must handle every constant.

walkthrough.title: Data classes and enums in practice

steps.do: Write a data class and use it.
steps.code:
data class Payment(val id: String, val amountCents: Long, val currency: String = "EUR")

fun main() {
    val p = Payment("p-1", 1_250)
    println(p)
    val refund = p.copy(amountCents = -1_250)
    println(refund == p)
    val (id, amount) = p
    println("$id: $amount")
}

lessons.title: Sealed classes and objects
objectives: Model results and states with sealed classes and interfaces
Use object declarations and companion objects
key_points: A sealed class or interface has a closed set of subclasses, all known when compiling (they must be in the same module and package), so a when over it can be exhaustive without an else branch.
Sealed hierarchies model results and states well: sealed interface PaymentResult with data class Approved(val reference: String), data class Declined(val reason: String) and data object Pending.
In a when branch such as is Declined ->, the value is smart-cast to that subclass, so its properties, such as reason, can be used directly.
An object declaration defines a class and its single instance at once, as in object Processor { ... }, which suits stateless helpers and shared state such as a counter.
A companion object holds members that belong to the class rather than to its instances, such as a factory function called as Payment.parse(line): the nearest thing in Kotlin to Java's static members.

steps.do: Declare a sealed interface with three implementations.
steps.code:

data class Approved(val reference: String) : PaymentResult
data class Declined(val reason: String) : PaymentResult
data object Pending : PaymentResult

modules.title: Coroutines, testing and Java interoperability
modules.summary: Run work concurrently with coroutines, test Kotlin code with kotlin.test, coroutines included, and mix Kotlin with Java: call each from the other, and convert Java files to Kotlin in the IDE.

lessons.title: Coroutines: suspend functions, launch and async
objectives: Explain what coroutines are and how they differ from threads
Write suspend functions and start coroutines with runBlocking, launch and async
Use structured concurrency and timeouts
key_points: A coroutine is a computation that can suspend, freeing its thread while it waits, and resume later. Coroutines are much lighter than threads, so a program can run very many of them on a few threads.
Coroutines come from the kotlinx.coroutines library, added to the build with implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core:..."); the language itself provides the suspend keyword.
A suspend function can pause without blocking its thread, as delay(500) does, and can only be called from a coroutine or from another suspend function.

runBlocking starts a coroutine and blocks the current thread until it finishes, which suits main and tests. launch starts a coroutine and returns a Job; async returns a Deferred, whose result you get with await().
Structured concurrency: coroutines run in a scope, such as coroutineScope { }, which waits for all its children and cancels the others if one of them fails.

withTimeoutOrNull(1_000) { ... } cancels a block that takes longer than a second and returns null instead, and withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } moves blocking work, such as reading files, to threads meant for it.

steps.do: Add the coroutines library to the dependencies in build.gradle.kts, then load the Gradle changes.

Run it.

lessons.title: Testing Kotlin with kotlin.test
objectives: Write and run tests with kotlin.test on JUnit 5
Test suspend functions with runTest
key_points: kotlin.test provides test annotations and assertions for Kotlin. With testImplementation(kotlin("test")) and tasks.test { useJUnitPlatform() } in build.gradle.kts, its tests run on JUnit 5.

A test class in src/test/kotlin has functions annotated with @Test that use assertions such as assertEquals(expected, actual), assertTrue, assertNull and assertFailsWith<IllegalArgumentException> { ... }.
Function names in backticks can contain spaces, so tests can read like sentences: fun `declines unsupported countries`().
runTest, from kotlinx-coroutines-test, runs a test's body in a coroutine and skips delays, so a test of code that waits for seconds finishes at once.
Gradle's test task runs every test and writes an HTML report to build/reports/tests/test/index.html; IntelliJ IDEA shows the same results in its test runner.

lessons.title: Kotlin and Java together
objectives: Call Java code from Kotlin, and Kotlin code from Java
Handle platform types safely
Convert Java files to Kotlin with IntelliJ IDEA
key_points: Kotlin calls Java directly: Java classes are used like Kotlin ones, without new, and getters and setters appear as properties, so customer.getEmail() is written customer.email.

Values from Java have platform types, shown as String!, because Kotlin can't know whether they can be null: decide by giving them a type, String or String?. Nullability annotations in the Java code, such as JetBrains' @Nullable and @NotNull, tell Kotlin.
Java sees a Kotlin property as a getter and a setter, and the top-level functions in Payments.kt as static methods of a class called PaymentsKt.

Annotations shape what Java sees: @JvmStatic makes a companion object's function a real static method, @JvmOverloads generates overloads for default arguments, and @JvmName renames a function or a file's class.

Code | Convert Java File to Kotlin File rewrites a Java file in Kotlin. Review the result: it behaves the same, but it isn't always idiomatic, and it may use !! or var where you'd choose a safe call or val.
Kotlin and Java files can sit side by side, in src/main/kotlin and src/main/java, so a project can move to Kotlin one file at a time, running its tests after each conversion.

walkthrough.title: Use Java from Kotlin, then convert it

steps.do: In the Project tool window, right-click src/main and choose New | Directory: IntelliJ IDEA suggests java, Gradle's folder for Java code. Create it and add a Java class to it.
Use it from Kotlin, in src/main/kotlin.
steps.code:
fun main() {
    val ana = Customer("Ana")
    ana.email = "ana@example.com"
    println("${ana.name} <${ana.email}>")
    val missing = Customer("Bruno").email
    println(missing?.length ?: "no email")
}

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: Ana <ana@example.com>, then no email.

steps.do: Put the caret on missing and open its quick documentation: its type is String!, a platform type.
Put the caret on email in the Kotlin code and go to its declaration: you land on the Java getter or setter.
Open Customer.java and choose Code | Convert Java File to Kotlin File.
steps.see: Customer.kt in place of Customer.java, with name and email as properties. Check which types it made nullable.

steps.do: Run main again to check that nothing changed.

lab.title: Convert a Java class to idiomatic Kotlin
lab.goal: Convert a Java class to Kotlin with IntelliJ IDEA, make it idiomatic, and prove with tests that it still behaves the same while Java code that uses it keeps compiling; then work out fees concurrently with coroutines and test that with runTest.
setup: IntelliJ IDEA and a Kotlin project built with Gradle, such as kotlin-basics, with kotlinx-coroutines-core and kotlinx-coroutines-test added as in the lessons
The starter files FeeCalculator.java and Checkout.java (in src/main/java/org/example) and FeeCalculatorTest.kt (in src/test/kotlin/org/example)

steps.do: Copy the starter files into the folders shown. If src/main/java doesn't exist yet, create it with New | Directory on src/main.
Run Checkout, a Java program, with the arrow beside its main method.
steps.see: Rate: 1.5% and three fee lines, ending with Fee on 10000 cents: 175 cents.

steps.do: Run FeeCalculatorTest, which tests the Java class from Kotlin.
steps.see: Tests passed: 6 of 6 tests.

steps.do: Open FeeCalculator.java and choose Code | Convert Java File to Kotlin File. If IntelliJ IDEA offers to correct code elsewhere in the project, accept.
steps.see: FeeCalculator.kt in place of the Java file.

steps.do: Run the tests and Checkout again: both should behave exactly as before. If Checkout no longer compiles, check that standard() is in a companion object and marked @JvmStatic.

Make the Kotlin idiomatic: a primary constructor with val properties, require in an init block, an expression body with a string template for describe, coerceAtLeast instead of Math.max, and roundToLong() instead of Math.round. Rerun the tests after each change.

Give minimumCents a default value of 50 and annotate the constructor with @JvmOverloads, so Java can leave it out. In Checkout.java, add a line that prints new FeeCalculator(2.0, 30).describe(5000), and run Checkout.
steps.see: Fee on 5000 cents: 130 cents

steps.do: Create Batch.kt in src/main/kotlin/org/example with package org.example and this function, which works out several fees concurrently, adding the kotlinx.coroutines imports with Show Context Actions.
Add a test with runTest that expects listOf(50L, 63L, 175L) from feesFor(FeeCalculator.standard(), listOf(1_000L, 2_500L, 10_000L)).
Right-click the src/test/kotlin folder and choose to run all the tests in it.
steps.see: Tests passed: 7 of 7 tests.

checks.text: FeeCalculator is now a Kotlin class, and every test passes.
Checkout.java, still in Java, prints the same fees as before.
The Kotlin is idiomatic: val properties in a primary constructor and require for validation, with no !!.
Java uses the Kotlin class through @JvmStatic and @JvmOverloads.
The fees are worked out concurrently with async and tested with runTest.

lab.submit: Paste your FeeCalculator.kt, Batch.kt and the new test, the output of Checkout and the test results, then a sentence on what the converter produced and what you changed by hand.
hints: Kotlin's version of Math.max for a lower limit is coerceAtLeast: fee.coerceAtLeast(minimumCents).
import kotlin.math.roundToLong gives Double.roundToLong(), which rounds halves up, as Math.round does.
An annotated primary constructor needs the constructor keyword: class FeeCalculator @JvmOverloads constructor(...).

project.title: Build a payment-processing pipeline
project.brief: Build a command-line payment processor in Kotlin with IntelliJ IDEA and Gradle. It reads a CSV file of payments and checks each line, reporting bad lines instead of crashing. It then checks the payments concurrently against a simulated risk service written with suspend functions, with a timeout so that one slow check can't hold up the rest. Model payments as data classes and outcomes as a sealed hierarchy (approved, declined with a reason, sent for review, timed out), handle every outcome with exhaustive when expressions, and print a report with totals per country and per outcome, built with collection operations. Include one Java class that the Kotlin code calls, such as an existing currency formatter, and make one Kotlin API pleasant to call from Java with @JvmStatic or @JvmOverloads. Test it with kotlin.test, including a coroutine test with runTest.
deliverables: The Gradle project: build.gradle.kts and the source code, with data classes, a sealed interface or class, and at least one object or companion object
Concurrent risk checks with coroutines (async or launch inside a coroutine scope), with a timeout for slow checks
A Java class that Kotlin calls, and a Kotlin API that Java calls
At least eight kotlin.test tests, including one with runTest and one that expects an exception
A sample payments CSV with at least ten lines, two of them invalid, and the report the program prints for it
A README.md that explains how to build, run and test the project

rubric.name: It works
rubric.description: The CSV is read, bad lines are reported, every payment gets an outcome, and the report's totals per country and per outcome are right.

rubric.name: Idiomatic Kotlin
rubric.description: val rather than var, null safety without !!, expression bodies and when expressions, and collection operations instead of hand-written loops where they read better.

rubric.name: Domain modelling
rubric.description: A sealed hierarchy models the outcomes, when expressions cover every case without else branches, and objects or companion objects are used where a single instance fits.

rubric.name: Coroutines
rubric.description: Checks run concurrently in a structured scope, slow checks time out without holding up the others, and there's no Thread.sleep or runBlocking inside suspend functions.

rubric.name: Java interoperability
rubric.description: A Java class is used from Kotlin, and a Kotlin API is called from Java, with @JvmStatic or @JvmOverloads where they help.

rubric.name: Tests and README
rubric.description: At least eight meaningful tests, including one with runTest and one that expects an exception, all passing, and a README that explains how to build, run and test.

project.submit: Paste your code (each file with its path), your tests, your README, the sample CSV, the report your program printed and the test results. A link to a public repository is welcome too.
